lessons.title: Parts of Speech and Sentence Structure
lessons.description: Understand the fundamental components of English sentences and their grammatical functions.
lessons.content:
English grammar is an important part of verbal ability assessments conducted during campus placements and recruitment examinations.

The eight traditional parts of speech are nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections.

1. Noun: Names a person, place, thing or idea.
Example: The developer completed the project.

2. Pronoun: Replaces a noun.
Example: She completed the assignment.

3. Verb: Expresses an action or state.
Example: The application runs successfully.

4. Adjective: Describes a noun or pronoun.
Example: He developed an efficient algorithm.

5. Adverb: Modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.
Example: The application runs efficiently.

6. Preposition: Expresses relationships involving time, place, direction or other connections.
Example: The interview starts at 10 AM.

7. Conjunction: Connects words, phrases or clauses.
Example: I know Java and Python.

8. Interjection: Expresses an immediate reaction.
Example: Wow! That was impressive.

Basic sentence structure:
Subject + Verb + Object.
Example: The student solved the problem.

Subject = The student.
Verb = solved.
Object = the problem.

Other common patterns include:
Subject + Verb: The server crashed.
Subject + Verb + Complement: The result is correct.
Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object: The trainer gave students feedback.

Sentence types:
Declarative: She completed the project.
Interrogative: Did she complete the project?
Imperative: Complete the project.
Exclamatory: What an excellent presentation!

Common placement errors:
Incorrect: He is a honest employee.
Correct: He is an honest employee.

Incorrect: She is good in Java.
Correct: She is good at Java.

Placement tip: Identify the subject, main verb and intended meaning before correcting a sentence.

lessons.title: Tenses and Verb Forms
lessons.description: Learn present, past and future tenses and their correct usage in verbal aptitude questions.
lessons.content:
Tenses indicate the time of an action or state. English also uses grammatical aspect to distinguish simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms.

Present Simple:
Structure: Subject + base verb, with -s or -es for most third-person singular subjects.
Example: She writes Java programs.

Present Continuous:
Structure: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing.
Example: She is preparing for an interview.

Present Perfect:
Structure: Subject + has/have + past participle.
Example: She has completed the assignment.

Present Perfect Continuous:
Structure: Subject + has/have been + verb-ing.
Example: She has been studying for two hours.

Past Simple:
Example: He attended the interview yesterday.

Past Continuous:
Example: He was studying when the recruiter called.

Past Perfect:
Example: The interview had started before he arrived.

Past Perfect Continuous:
Example: She had been working for three hours before the break.

Future Simple:
Example: I will attend the interview tomorrow.

Future Continuous:
Example: I will be preparing at 8 PM.

Future Perfect:
Example: I will have completed the course by Friday.

Future Perfect Continuous:
Example: By December, she will have been working here for two years.

Important rules:
1. Use the past simple for completed actions at a specified past time.
2. Use the present perfect when a past event has a relevant connection to the present and no finished past-time expression is specified.
3. Use the past perfect to clarify an action completed before another past event.
4. Use 'since' for a starting point and 'for' for a duration.

Incorrect: I have completed my degree last year.
Correct: I completed my degree last year.

Incorrect: She is working here since 2022.
Correct: She has been working here since 2022.

Placement tip: Time expressions such as yesterday, since, for, already, by and tomorrow help identify the appropriate tense.

lessons.title: Subject-Verb Agreement and Articles
lessons.description: Understand agreement rules, determiners and correct usage of a, an and the.
lessons.content:
Subject-verb agreement means that a verb must agree with its subject in number and person.

Singular subject:
The student works hard.

Plural subject:
The students work hard.

Common rules:
1. He, she and it usually take a verb ending in -s or -es in the present simple.
2. I and you take the base verb form in the present simple.
3. A phrase between the subject and verb usually does not change agreement.
4. Subjects connected by 'and' generally take a plural verb when they refer to separate people or things.
5. Words such as everyone, somebody and each normally take singular agreement.

Examples:
Correct: Each student has a laptop.
Correct: The list of candidates is ready.
Correct: The manager and the developer are attending the meeting.

Either-or and neither-nor constructions commonly use agreement with the nearer subject in formal placement grammar exercises.

Example: Neither the manager nor the employees are available.
Example: Neither the employees nor the manager is available.

Articles:
A is used before a consonant sound.
An is used before a vowel sound.
The identifies something specific or already known.

Examples:
A university, because university begins with a consonant /y/ sound.
An hour, because hour begins with a vowel sound.
An engineer.
The employee who submitted the report.

Incorrect: She is an university student.
Correct: She is a university student.

Incorrect: Everyone have submitted the form.
Correct: Everyone has submitted the form.

Placement tip: Determine the true subject rather than the noun closest to the verb.

lessons.title: Prepositions, Conjunctions and Modifiers
lessons.description: Learn correct word relationships, sentence connections and modifier placement.
lessons.content:
Prepositions express relationships between words and phrases.

Common prepositions include in, on, at, by, with, from, to, for, between and among.

Time expressions:
At 9 AM.
On Monday.
In October.
Since 2023.
For three years.

Place expressions:
At the office.
In Bengaluru.
On the table.

Common verb-preposition combinations:
Depend on.
Interested in.
Responsible for.
Good at.
Apply for a job.

Conjunctions connect ideas.

Coordinating conjunctions include for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so.

Example: She prepared well, but she was nervous.

Subordinating conjunctions include because, although, while, if, unless and since.

Example: Although the question was difficult, he solved it.

Correlative conjunctions include either...or, neither...nor and not only...but also.

Example: She knows both Java and Python.

Modifiers provide additional information about words or phrases. Incorrect placement can change meaning.

Ambiguous: She almost completed all the assignments.
Clearer: She completed almost all the assignments.

The first sentence may suggest that she came close to completing them without actually doing so. The second clearly means that most assignments were completed.

Parallel structure requires related elements to follow a consistent grammatical pattern.

Incorrect: She enjoys coding, testing and to design applications.
Correct: She enjoys coding, testing and designing applications.

Placement tip: For sentence correction, check prepositions, conjunction pairs, modifier placement and parallel structure.

lessons.title: Error Detection, Sentence Correction and Voice
lessons.description: Practice identifying grammatical errors, improving sentences and converting active and passive voice.
lessons.content:
Error detection and sentence correction are common verbal aptitude question types.

A reliable correction process is:
1. Identify the subject and main verb.
2. Check subject-verb agreement.
3. Verify tense consistency.
4. Examine articles and prepositions.
5. Check pronouns and modifiers.
6. Ensure the corrected sentence preserves the intended meaning.

Example 1:
Incorrect: He do not know the answer.
Correct: He does not know the answer.

Example 2:
Incorrect: She has went to the office.
Correct: She has gone to the office.

Example 3:
Incorrect: I am senior than him.
Correct: I am senior to him.

Example 4:
Incorrect: The informations are useful.
Correct: The information is useful.

Active voice places the subject performing the action in focus.
Example: The developer fixed the bug.

Passive voice places the affected object in subject position.
Example: The bug was fixed by the developer.

Passive construction commonly uses an appropriate form of 'be' plus the past participle.

Present simple:
Active: The team reviews the code.
Passive: The code is reviewed by the team.

Past simple:
Active: The tester identified the issue.
Passive: The issue was identified by the tester.

Future simple:
Active: The manager will announce the result.
Passive: The result will be announced by the manager.

Direct and indirect speech:
Direct: He said, 'I am ready.'
Indirect: He said that he was ready.

Reported speech changes depend on reporting context, time reference and whether the information remains true.

Placement tip: Do not change a grammatically correct sentence simply because an alternative wording sounds more formal.

quizzes.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence.
options: She go to college every day.
She goes to college every day.
She going to college every day.
She gone to college every day.
quizzes.explanation: The third-person singular subject 'she' takes 'goes' in the present simple.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct article: He is ___ honest employee.
quizzes.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so 'an' is appropriate.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct verb: Each of the students ___ a laptop.
Fill in the blank: She has been working here ___ 2022.
quizzes.explanation: 'Since' introduces the starting point of an action continuing into the present.

quizzes.question: Identify the correct past tense sentence.
options: He has attended the interview yesterday.
He had attend the interview yesterday.
quizzes.explanation: The past simple is appropriate for a completed action at the specified past time 'yesterday'.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct preposition: She is interested ___ software development.
Choose the sentence with correct parallel structure.
options: He likes coding, testing and to debug.
He likes coding, testing and debugging.
He likes code, testing and to debug.
He likes coding, to test and debugging.
quizzes.explanation: Coding, testing and debugging use parallel -ing forms.

quizzes.question: Select the correct passive voice of: The developer fixed the bug.
options: The bug was fixed by the developer.
The bug is fixing by the developer.
The developer was fixed by the bug.
quizzes.explanation: Past simple passive uses 'was/were + past participle'.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Neither the manager nor the employees is available.
Neither the manager nor the employees are available.
Neither the manager nor the employees has available.
Neither the manager nor the employees was available yesterday are.
quizzes.explanation: With neither...nor, formal placement grammar commonly uses agreement with the nearer subject. 'Employees' is plural, so 'are' is used.

quizzes.question: Choose the correct sentence using the present perfect.
quizzes.explanation: The present perfect uses 'has/have + past participle'. The past participle of 'write' is 'written'.

exercises.title: Identify Parts of Speech
exercises.description: Recognize grammatical functions in a professional sentence.
exercises.instructions: Identify the parts of speech of the words 'skilled', 'developer', 'quickly', 'fixed' and 'the' in this sentence: 'The skilled developer quickly fixed the application.' Explain the function of each word.

exercises.title: Tense Correction Practice
exercises.description: Correct errors involving tense and verb forms.
exercises.instructions: Correct these sentences and explain each correction: (1) She has completed her degree last year. (2) I am learning Java since January. (3) He has went to the office. (4) They was preparing for the interview. (5) She will completed the task tomorrow.

exercises.title: Subject-Verb Agreement Challenge
exercises.description: Choose correct verbs for singular, plural and compound subjects.
exercises.instructions: Fill in the correct verbs: (1) Each student ___ a resume. (has/have) (2) The list of candidates ___ ready. (is/are) (3) Neither the trainer nor the students ___ absent. (is/are) (4) The manager and the developer ___ attending. (is/are) (5) Everyone ___ submitted the form. (has/have).

exercises.title: Sentence Improvement and Error Detection
exercises.description: Improve grammatical accuracy and professional clarity.
exercises.instructions: Rewrite these sentences correctly: (1) He is good in Java. (2) She is an university student. (3) The informations are useful. (4) He do not understand the question. (5) She enjoys coding, testing and to design applications. Explain the error in each sentence.

exercises.title: Placement Grammar Assessment
exercises.description: Practice advanced grammar, voice and reported speech.
exercises.instructions: Complete the following tasks: (1) Convert 'The team reviews the code' into passive voice. (2) Convert 'The tester identified the issue' into passive voice. (3) Rewrite 'He said, I am ready' using reported speech, assuming the reporting context requires tense backshift. (4) Correct 'Neither the employees nor the manager are available.' (5) Explain the difference between 'She worked here for three years' and 'She has worked here for three years'.
